definition: Charm and skill at attracting or impressing someone, especially a romantic interest.
meanings: As a verb, to charm someone ("she rizzed him up").
example: He got her number with pure rizz.
exampleTranslation: He got her number with pure charm.
context: Playful and widely understood; usually about flirting, but kids also use it for general charisma. Shortened from "charisma".
era: approx. 2021–2023 (named Oxford Word of the Year 2023)
origin: Clipped from "charisma"; popularized by streamers and short-form video creators before going mainstream.

definition: A win or a good outcome; shorthand for something that went well.
meanings: Said as a reaction to praise someone ("W take").
example: Got an A on my science project, big W.
exampleTranslation: I got an A on my science project, a great win.
context: Borrowed from sports win/loss records. Written as a capital letter; can be dropped into almost any sentence.
origin: From the "W" in win-loss records; spread through sports talk, streaming and social media.

definition: A loss, failure or embarrassing outcome.
meanings: "Take the L" means accept a loss gracefully.
example: I forgot my lunch and my homework today. Massive L.
exampleTranslation: I forgot my lunch and my homework today. A big failure.
context: Opposite of W. Often used jokingly about small mishaps; can feel harsh if aimed at someone else.
era: approx. 1990s as "loser" gesture; widespread online approx. 2010s
origin: From "loss"/"loser" in sports; the hand-on-forehead "L" gesture has been used for decades.
mistakes: Calling someone an L to their face is often read as an insult, not a joke.

definition: A lie or exaggeration; to cap is to lie or brag falsely.
meanings: "That's cap" means "that's not true."
example: You ran a mile in four minutes? That's cap.
exampleTranslation: You ran a mile in four minutes? That is a lie.
context: Said to call out a fib, usually playfully; the opposite is "no cap".
origin: Rooted in African American Vernacular English (AAVE) and hip-hop; earlier meanings of "cap" as bragging or lying appear in Black communities before going viral online.

definition: "No lie" or "I'm being honest"; used to stress that a statement is true.
example: This pizza is the best I've ever had, no cap.
exampleTranslation: This pizza is the best I've ever had, honestly.
context: Added at the end of a claim to show sincerity.
origin: From AAVE and hip-hop; popularized widely via rap lyrics and social media.

definition: An agreement or confirmation: "okay," "deal," or "sounds good."
meanings: Can also be a challenge: "Bet." meaning "prove it" depending on tone.
example: "Meet at the library at four?" "Bet."
exampleTranslation: "Meet at the library at four?" "Okay, sounds good."
context: Short, casual agreement; tone decides whether it means yes or a dare.
origin: Rooted in AAVE; related to the older sense of "you bet."

definition: A way to agree or accept without needing more explanation.
example: You need a ride to practice? Say less.
exampleTranslation: You need a ride to practice? Understood, I'll take you.
context: Implies "you already convinced me." Often used to confirm plans.
origin: Used in hip-hop and Black online communities; hedge: exact origin unclear.

definition: Short for "for real"; shows sincerity or agreement.
meanings: Used alone as a reply meaning "I agree" or "really?"
example: That test was so hard, fr.
exampleTranslation: That test was really hard, honestly.
context: Doubling it ("fr fr") adds emphasis. Appears in texts and speech.
origin: Abbreviation of "for real"; popular in Black online communities and then broadly.

definition: "On God": a swear that what you are saying is true.
example: I didn't take your charger, ong.
exampleTranslation: I didn't take your charger, I swear.
context: Used to show you are serious. Some people find invoking God casually disrespectful.
origin: From AAVE and hip-hop; echoes older phrases like "swear to God."
sensitiveNote: Contains a religious reference used casually; some families or teachers may prefer it not be used.

definition: Seriously or truly; used to stress sincerity.
meanings: As a question: "Deadass?" means "Are you serious?"
example: Deadass, I forgot it was Friday.
exampleTranslation: Seriously, I forgot it was Friday.
context: Strongly tied to New York City speech but now used widely.
era: approx. 1990s in NYC; broader approx. late 2010s
origin: Associated with New York City English and AAVE, including Black and Latino communities; hedge: precise origin not settled.
sensitiveNote: Contains the word "ass" as a compound, so some schools treat it as mild profanity.

definition: Somewhat or secretly; a quiet, understated degree of something.
meanings: Describes something kept discreet.
example: I low-key want to go home early.
exampleTranslation: I kind of want to go home early.
context: Softens a feeling or confession. Opposite is "high-key".
origin: Rooted in older AAVE usage and hip-hop; later spread widely online.

definition: Very much or openly; the loud version of "low-key".
example: I high-key love this song.
exampleTranslation: I really love this song.
context: Used for strong, unhidden feelings.
origin: Counterpart to "low-key"; popular in Black and youth culture online.

definition: An all-purpose reaction showing disbelief, disappointment or amusement.
meanings: Also a casual address for a friend.
example: Bruh, you spilled juice on the couch again?
exampleTranslation: Oh come on, you spilled juice on the couch again?
context: The meaning depends on tone: disbelief, annoyance, amusement or simply "hey".
origin: Variation of "bro"; popular in AAVE and US youth speech.

definition: Casual word for a male friend, or any person, used as an address or filler.
meanings: Used by many genders as a general "dude."
example: Bro, you have to try this game.
exampleTranslation: Dude, you have to try this game.
context: Casual address among friends; it is no longer only about brothers or boys.
origin: Short for "brother", used in many communities including AAVE and surfer/college culture.

definition: Suspicious or questionable.
example: The teacher left the room and the door locked? That's sus.
exampleTranslation: The teacher left the room and the door locked? That's suspicious.
context: Often playful. "Sus" was shortened from "suspect"/"suspicious" long before it blew up.
origin: Clipped from "suspect"/"suspicious"; short forms used earlier in British and US slang; popularized via the game Among Us around 2020.

definition: Mediocre or average; not good, not bad.
meanings: Mildly dismissive.
example: The movie was mid, honestly.
exampleTranslation: The movie was mediocre, honestly.
context: Sounds harsher than "okay". Usually aimed at things, not people.
origin: Clipped from "middle" or "mediocre"; popularized in online and Black social-media communities.

definition: Excellent or really impressive, especially music, outfits or ideas.
example: Your new shoes are fire.
exampleTranslation: Your new shoes are excellent.
context: Safe compliment among friends; often paired with the flame emoji.
origin: Rooted in hip-hop and AAVE ("hot" and "fire" for excellent).

definition: Exciting, fun or excellent; a lively party or event is lit.
meanings: Older slang sense: intoxicated.
example: That concert was lit.
exampleTranslation: That concert was exciting.
context: Many teens now find this term dated, though it is still widely understood.
origin: Rooted in AAVE and hip-hop; earlier senses include "drunk".
sensitiveNote: Older uses meant intoxicated; current "exciting" sense is mild.

definition: To be really good, usually about songs or food.
example: This new playlist slaps.
exampleTranslation: This new playlist is really good.
context: "Slaps" works like "hits" in older speech. Mostly about music.
origin: Developed in hip-hop and online music communities.

definition: Extremely good, especially food.
example: Mom's lasagna is bussin'.
exampleTranslation: Mom's lasagna is delicious.
context: Mostly used for food; adding an apostrophe is optional.
origin: Rooted in AAVE (from "bursting"/"busting"); popularized via TikTok and rap.

definition: Acceptable, reasonable or worthy of respect.
meanings: "Valid" as a reply means "that makes sense."
example: You wanting a nap after school? Valid.
exampleTranslation: You wanting a nap after school? That makes sense.
context: Used to affirm someone's feelings or choices.
origin: Standard word extended in social media and Black youth culture.

definition: Authentic, unbothered by others' opinions and true to yourself.
meanings: Also strongly political in some online circles.
example: Wearing the old jacket to prom was based.
exampleTranslation: Wearing the old jacket to prom was bold and genuine.
context: Context matters: in some internet spaces "based" is tied to political arguments.
origin: Popularized by Bay Area rapper Lil B ("Based God"); hedge: earlier senses. Later adopted by political online communities.
sensitiveNote: Often carries political connotations online; check context before using.

definition: Awkward or embarrassing to watch or hear about.
meanings: Also a noun and a verb ("I cringed").
example: His old videos are so cringe.
exampleTranslation: His old videos are so embarrassing.
context: Can feel mean when aimed at someone's sincere effort.
origin: Standard verb "cringe" turned into an adjective on internet forums.

definition: Being the greatest of all time; the best at something.
example: Our coach is goated.
exampleTranslation: Our coach is the greatest.
context: Used for athletes, artists, foods, friends. Pronounced "goat".
origin: GOAT acronym is often linked to Muhammad Ali and hip-hop; "goated" adjective popular online.

definition: To do something exceptionally well or look fantastic.
meanings: Used as an exclamation of praise.
example: You slayed that presentation.
exampleTranslation: You did that presentation amazingly well.
context: Works for looks or performance. Cheerful.
origin: Developed in Black and Latino LGBTQ+ ballroom and drag culture before mainstream pop adoption.

definition: Performed perfectly; did something flawlessly.
meanings: "Left no crumbs" emphasizes total perfection.
example: She ate that solo, no crumbs.
exampleTranslation: She performed that solo perfectly.
context: Praise for performance, style or comebacks.
origin: From Black and LGBTQ+ ballroom, drag and Black Twitter culture; popularized by pop-culture online.

definition: A spelled-out "period" meaning "end of discussion."
example: I am not eating broccoli, periodt.
exampleTranslation: I am not eating broccoli, and that is final.
context: Spelled with a "t" in texts to add attitude and finality.
origin: AAVE and Black Twitter; a variant of "period."

definition: Said after a statement to show it is final, no debate.
example: Pizza is the best Friday dinner, period.
exampleTranslation: Pizza is the best Friday dinner, end of story.
context: Used at the end of a sentence to say there is nothing more to argue.
origin: AAVE and standard English emphasis; "periodt" is stylized.

definition: Used to say something gives off a particular vibe: "it's giving ___".
example: That sweater is giving cozy cabin.
exampleTranslation: That sweater has the feel of a cozy cabin.
context: Followed by a noun or style. Can be a compliment or a gentle tease.
origin: Rooted in Black and Latino LGBTQ+ ballroom and drag culture; popularized by Black Twitter and TikTok.

definition: Acting or feeling like the star of your own story, confident and a bit dramatic.
example: She walked in with main character energy.
exampleTranslation: She walked in with confident star-of-the-show attitude.
context: Positive when about confidence; mocking when about selfishness.
origin: Popularized on TikTok and Twitter; earlier use in film/writing terms.

definition: A reaction to something awkward, embarrassing or cringeworthy.
example: He announced the wrong name? Big yikes.
exampleTranslation: He announced the wrong name? That is really awkward.
context: "Yikes" is old; "big yikes" amplifies it and is often tongue-in-cheek.
origin: "Yikes" is long-established; "big yikes" spread online.

definition: Behaving or speaking in an extreme, shocking, or inappropriate way.
meanings: Also, in some regions, not at home or unreachable.
example: Saying that to the teacher was out of pocket.
exampleTranslation: Saying that to the teacher was out of line.
context: Used for behavior that crosses a line; can also describe jokes that went too far.
origin: From AAVE; older sense of "out of reach."

definition: Caught clearly doing something wrong, with undeniable proof.
example: He skipped practice and got caught in 4K.
exampleTranslation: He skipped practice and got caught red-handed.
context: The "4K" refers to ultra-high-definition video, suggesting the evidence is crystal clear.
origin: Popularized by social media and Black Twitter; hedge.

definition: Something that keeps popping into your mind without your permission.
example: That song lives rent-free in my head.
exampleTranslation: That song is stuck in my head.
context: Used for annoying or exciting thoughts that keep returning.
origin: Popularized online; earlier everyday phrase.

definition: A sudden feeling of disgust or turn-off toward someone you liked.
meanings: Used casually for something suddenly unappealing.
example: He chewed with his mouth open and I got the ick.
exampleTranslation: He chewed with his mouth open and I suddenly lost interest.
context: Usually about romance but also used jokingly.
era: approx. 2010s; popularized via UK reality TV and TikTok around 2018–2023
origin: Popularized by UK reality dating TV (hedge).

definition: Telling someone to spend less time online and go outside.
example: You've been gaming for 10 hours, touch grass.
exampleTranslation: You've been gaming for 10 hours, go outside.
context: Mocking or caring depending on tone.
origin: Online gaming culture.
sensitiveNote: Often used to put someone down; be kind about it.

definition: Give someone space to do their thing without interrupting.
example: He's drawing; let him cook.
exampleTranslation: He's drawing; give him space to work.
context: Said when you want others to stay quiet while someone is working or creating; can be a sincere show of support or a joke.
origin: Popularized online around streaming and sports (hedge).

definition: In deep trouble or defeated; doomed.
example: I forgot my project at home; I'm cooked.
exampleTranslation: I forgot my project at home; I'm doomed.
context: Used when a situation is hopeless, such as a looming deadline.
origin: Online and gaming (hedge).

definition: To focus fully on a goal.
example: Finals week: time to lock in.
exampleTranslation: Finals week: time to focus hard.
context: Typically said before studying, training or a big task.
origin: Sports and online communities.

definition: Following through and doing what you said, with confidence.
example: She said she'd win and she stood on business.
exampleTranslation: She said she'd win and she followed through.
context: Praise for sticking to your word and showing up.
origin: Popularized in Black and sports social media (hedge).

definition: An expression of admiration or amazement.
example: Sheesh, that shot was perfect.
exampleTranslation: Wow, that shot was perfect.
context: Used for admiration or surprise; the stretched spelling "sheeesh" is common.
origin: A softened version of "jeez"; popularized online.

definition: Brutally bold, usually in a funny or impressive way.
example: Your comeback was savage.
exampleTranslation: Your comeback was ruthlessly good.
context: Said when someone does something bold, blunt or ruthless in an impressive way.
origin: Hip-hop and online use.
sensitiveNote: Original meaning is cruel or violent.

definition: Bitter or annoyed, especially after losing.
example: He's salty about the game.
exampleTranslation: He's bitter about the game.
context: Used when someone is bitter, usually after a loss or an unfair outcome.
origin: Gaming and AAVE usage.

definition: Shocked or deeply unsettled.
example: I'm shook that you finished.
exampleTranslation: I'm shocked that you finished.
context: Used when something unexpected shakes you; considered a bit older now.
origin: AAVE and Black queer culture.

definition: Gossip or juicy news.
example: Spill the tea about the field trip!
exampleTranslation: Tell me the gossip about the field trip!
context: Used when sharing or asking for juicy news; can lean toward gossip, which can hurt others.
origin: Black drag and LGBTQ+ ballroom culture ("T" for truth).
sensitiveNote: Gossip can hurt people; use kindly.

definition: To show off.
example: He's flexing his new shoes.
exampleTranslation: He's showing off his new shoes.
context: Can be a neutral joke or a criticism of boasting.

definition: Something relatable.
example: Monday mornings are a big mood.
exampleTranslation: Monday mornings are so relatable.
context: Used as a reply to relatable posts, often meaning "I feel the same".
origin: Popularized by Black Twitter.

definition: The feeling or atmosphere of something.
meanings: "Vibe check": assess the mood.
example: This cafe has great vibes.
exampleTranslation: This cafe has a great atmosphere.
context: "Vibe check" can be a playful test of someone's mood or character.
origin: Clipped from "vibrations"; counterculture then Black and online use.

definition: Over the top.
example: Bringing a banner to a quiz? So extra.
exampleTranslation: Bringing a banner to a quiz? So over the top.
context: Teasing or admiring depending on tone; implies doing more than needed.
origin: AAVE and Black Twitter.

definition: When replies get more engagement than the original post.
example: His post got ratioed.
exampleTranslation: His post got far more replies than likes, a sign people disagreed.
context: Used mostly on X/Twitter: if replies outnumber likes, people say the post got ratioed, meaning it was unpopular.

definition: Feels special or better than usual.
example: Pizza on Friday hits different.
exampleTranslation: Pizza on Friday feels special.
context: Used for experiences that feel more intense or satisfying than normal.

definition: A catchy song.
example: This song is a bop.
exampleTranslation: This song is a great song.
context: Used for catchy, enjoyable songs; the sense of a "bop" as a song is common in pop fandoms.
origin: Stan Twitter and hip-hop.

definition: Expresses disbelief or impossibility.
example: No shot you got tickets.
exampleTranslation: No way you got tickets.
context: Used when something seems impossible or too good to be true.
origin: Gaming and online.

definition: Okay.
example: Aight, see you later.
exampleTranslation: Okay, see you later.
context: Quick agreement or a way to sign off; shortened and softened pronunciation of "alright".
origin: AAVE pronunciation of "alright".

definition: Acting wildly or irrationally.
example: You're tweaking if you think that works.
exampleTranslation: You're acting crazy if you think that works.
context: Used for someone acting wild, nonsensical or overreacting.
origin: AAVE; origin tied to stimulant drug use.
sensitiveNote: Origin relates to drug use; kids often use it just for silly behavior.

definition: Hyper excited.
example: I'm geeked for the game.
exampleTranslation: I'm hyped for the game.
context: Used for being fired up or overly excited; the term also appears in drug-related contexts.
origin: AAVE; origin drug-related.
sensitiveNote: Original sense referred to being high; current use is mostly "excited".

definition: Be fucking for real; stop being ridiculous.
example: Bffr, that is not real.
exampleTranslation: Be serious, that is not real.
context: Used when someone says something unbelievable; because of the swear word, keep out of school settings.
sensitiveNote: Stands for a phrase containing profanity.

definition: "All of that"; used to mock a long message.
example: Didn't read allat.
exampleTranslation: I didn't read all of that.
context: Mockingly implies a message was too long; used jokingly, but rude to someone sharing something serious.

definition: Very, or a lot of.
example: It was hella hot.
exampleTranslation: It was very hot.
context: Northern California regional intensifier; spread widely through 1990s–2000s pop culture.
origin: Northern California / Bay Area.
sensitiveNote: Contraction of "hell of a", considered mild.

definition: About to; fixing to.
example: I'm finna leave.
exampleTranslation: I'm about to leave.
context: Used as a helping word before a verb to mean "about to"; a feature of AAVE and Southern speech.
origin: AAVE and Southern US English.

definition: Very (New York slang).
example: It's mad cold.
exampleTranslation: It's very cold.
context: In NYC, "mad" before an adjective or noun means "very" or "a lot of"; not about anger in this sense.

definition: Very (New England).
example: It's wicked cold.
exampleTranslation: It's very cold.
context: Used before an adjective in New England, especially Massachusetts, to mean "very". Not about evil.

definition: You all.
example: Y'all ready?
exampleTranslation: Are you all ready?
context: Southern.

definition: Very, or a lot of (UK).
example: There's bare people here.
exampleTranslation: There are loads of people here.
context: In UK urban English, "bare" modifies a noun or adjective to mean "a lot" or "very".

definition: Attractive or great (UK).
example: That meal was peng.
exampleTranslation: That meal was great.
context: UK slang with sense of "great" or "attractive", used for food, looks, or experiences.

definition: Isn't it.
example: Cold today, innit?
exampleTranslation: It's cold today, isn't it?
context: Contraction of "isn't it"; in UK speech it can be a tag question or a general agreement word.

definition: What's going on?
example: Wagwan, how are you?
exampleTranslation: What's up, how are you?
context: A casual greeting heard in the UK, especially London, now used in online UK culture and by others.
origin: Jamaican Patois via UK.

definition: Close friend.
example: Thanks, fam.
exampleTranslation: Thanks, friend.
context: Friendly address for friends or close acquaintances; in the UK it can sound like "mate".

definition: Major improvement.
example: Her glow up was amazing.
exampleTranslation: Her improvement was amazing.
context: Used for visible transformations, such as style, confidence, skills, or growth.

definition: Underrated.
example: That band is slept on.
exampleTranslation: That band is underrated.
context: Describes something talented or good that has not received enough attention.

definition: Immediately, or "for sure".
example: Pizza? On sight.
exampleTranslation: Pizza? Right away.
context: Used as an eager "yes" to an offer, such as "free pizza? On sight."
sensitiveNote: Original sense was a threat of violence.

definition: Strong agreement.
example: Pizza is the best. Say it louder.
exampleTranslation: Pizza is the best. Exactly right.
context: Used to cheer on a statement you strongly agree with.

definition: Highlights a detail.
plain: what stands out to me is
example: It's the glitter for me.
exampleTranslation: What stands out to me is the glitter.
context: Fill in the blank with the detail that stands out, such as "it's the sparkles for me".

definition: Introduces a funny story.
example: The way I tripped.
exampleTranslation: I can't believe how I tripped.
context: Opens a self-deprecating or dramatic story, often cut off mid-sentence for comic effect.

definition: I just burst out laughing.
example: IJBOL at that meme.
exampleTranslation: I just burst out laughing at that meme.
context: Texting abbreviation for laughing suddenly; a variation on LOL.

definition: Too amused.
example: I'm weak, that was funny.
exampleTranslation: That was hilarious.
context: A reaction to something hilarious, as if laughter made you too weak to cope.

definition: Laughing hard.
example: I'm dead, that is so funny.
exampleTranslation: That is hilarious.
context: Said when something is extremely funny; skull emoji often appears. Not literal, but be thoughtful around real loss or grief.
sensitiveNote: Not literal; be careful around real grief.

definition: Don't overthink.
example: It's not that deep.
exampleTranslation: Don't overthink it.
context: Used to reassure someone or to wave off overanalyzing; can sound dismissive if the person is genuinely upset.

definition: Bothered.
example: Why you pressed?
exampleTranslation: Why are you upset?
context: Teasing tone toward someone who seems bothered; "stay pressed" is a playful jab that can sound dismissive.

definition: Relaxed.
example: He's chill.
exampleTranslation: He's relaxed.
context: Describes a person or situation that is easygoing; also a command ("chill out"). Fine for nearly any informal setting.

definition: Money or opportunity.
example: Secure the bag.
exampleTranslation: Go get success.
context: "Secure the bag" means pursue money, success or a good opportunity; used jokingly for small wins too.

definition: Win.
example: That is a dub.
exampleTranslation: That is a win.
context: Equivalent of "W"; used for any win, from games to good news. Pronounced like the word "dub".

definition: Real, genuine or really good.
meanings: As an adverb, "really" ("that was legit scary").
example: This bakery is legit the best in town.
exampleTranslation: This bakery is genuinely the best in town.
context: Clipped from "legitimate"; works in casual speech and texts.
origin: Clipped from "legitimate"; established in US English for many decades.

definition: Fancy or acting upper-class, often with a teasing tone.
example: Oat milk lattes are a little bougie.
exampleTranslation: Oat milk lattes are a little fancy.
context: Playful about luxury tastes; can be mildly mocking.
era: term older; popularized widely in the 2010s by hip-hop
origin: Respelling of "bourgeois", used in Black American English and hip-hop.

definition: To fire back a sharp, witty reply to criticism.
example: She clapped back at the rumor with one great tweet.
exampleTranslation: She responded sharply to the rumor with one great post.
context: Admiring when the reply is clever; can imply conflict.
origin: Associated with Black social media and hip-hop; hedge on exact origin.

definition: Proof, usually screenshots or recordings that back up a claim.
example: If you say he lied, bring the receipts.
exampleTranslation: If you say he lied, show the proof.
context: Used when someone demands or shows evidence.
origin: Popularized in Black online communities and pop culture; hedge.

definition: Excited and energetic, or to build excitement.
meanings: As a verb: "hype someone up" means to cheer them on.
example: I'm so hyped for the field trip!
exampleTranslation: I'm so excited for the field trip!
context: Clipped from "hyperbole"/"hyperactive"; used widely for events and people.
origin: Clipped form used in US advertising and hip-hop; origin loosely traced.

definition: Very happy and excited.
example: We're stoked about the beach trip.
exampleTranslation: We're thrilled about the beach trip.
context: Friendly and upbeat; associated with surf and skate culture.
origin: Associated with California surf and skate culture.

definition: A flexible word for any thing, person or place.
example: Hand me that jawn on the table.
exampleTranslation: Hand me that thing on the table.
context: Strongly associated with Philadelphia and nearby areas.
origin: Philadelphia, associated with Black Philadelphia speech; likely a variant of "joint". Hedge.

definition: Bad, lame or unfair.
example: It's wack that practice got canceled.
exampleTranslation: It's unfair that practice got canceled.
context: Sounds a bit older to many teens.

definition: Very or a lot of; a milder cousin of "hella".
example: It was hecka crowded at the fair.
exampleTranslation: It was very crowded at the fair.
context: A family-friendly cousin of "hella" popular in Northern California.
origin: Northern California; a softened variant of "hella".

definition: Awesome or impressive.
example: That mural is dope.
exampleTranslation: That mural is awesome.
context: Sounds a bit older now but is still widely understood.
origin: Hip-hop and AAVE; the older meaning is drugs.
sensitiveNote: The word also means illegal drugs; school staff may react to it.

definition: Poorly made, glitchy or unreliable.
example: My laptop is so janky today.
exampleTranslation: My laptop is so unreliable today.
context: Works for tech, cars, or anything poorly made.
origin: Origin uncertain; used widely in American English and gaming.

definition: A small exclamation for a bump, a surprise or "excuse me".
example: Ope, let me just squeeze past you.
exampleTranslation: Oops, excuse me while I squeeze past you.
context: Midwestern politeness marker.
origin: Associated with the American Midwest.

definition: You all (Pittsburgh).
example: Are yinz coming to the game?
exampleTranslation: Are you all coming to the game?
context: Used mainly in Pittsburgh; "yinzer" is a nickname for local people.
origin: Pittsburgh and western Pennsylvania.

definition: Encouragement to speak passionately or perform boldly.
example: You have strong opinions about pizza? Go off.
exampleTranslation: You have strong opinions about pizza? Go for it.
context: Supportive, often teasing.
origin: Associated with Black Twitter and LGBTQ+ culture; hedge.

definition: Trying to.
example: I'm tryna finish before lunch.
exampleTranslation: I'm trying to finish before lunch.
context: Spelling mirrors speech; appears in casual texts and lyrics.
origin: Reduced pronunciation common in AAVE and informal US English.

definition: Friendly term for a buddy.
example: Dawg, that was a good game.
exampleTranslation: Buddy, that was a good game.
context: Friendly between close friends.
origin: Hip-hop and AAVE; spelling mimics Southern and Black pronunciation.

definition: A close friend.
example: He's my homie from third grade.
exampleTranslation: He's my close friend from third grade.
context: Friendly.
origin: Chicano and hip-hop cultures, spreading widely.

definition: So memorable it becomes a symbol; used for admiration.
example: That halftime show was iconic.
exampleTranslation: That halftime show was unforgettable.
context: Compliment for people, outfits and moments.
origin: Standard English adjective, popularized in pop culture and LGBTQ+ communities.

definition: A situation so disappointing or silly that "bruh" is the only reaction.
example: Walking into the glass door was a bruh moment.
exampleTranslation: Walking into the glass door was a facepalm moment.
context: Used for awkward, silly events.
origin: Built on "bruh"; popularized online.

definition: To perform spectacularly, or to speak boldly.
example: She popped off at the talent show.
exampleTranslation: She went all out at the talent show.
context: Praise for energy.
origin: Associated with Black and online culture; hedge.
